content: Alpha-lactalbumin, also referred to as LALBA, is a protein encoded by the LALBA gene in humans. Function Alpha-lactalbumin plays a critical role in regulating lactose production in the milk of nearly all mammalian species. In primates, the expression of alpha-lactalbumin is upregulated in response to the hormone prolactin, which subsequently enhances lactose production. This protein serves as the regulatory subunit of the lactose synthase (LS) heterodimer, while beta-1,4-galactosyltransferase (beta4Gal-T1) acts as the catalytic component. Together, these proteins enable lactose synthase to synthesize lactose by transferring galactose moieties to glucose. As a multimer, alpha-lactalbumin exhibits a strong binding affinity for calcium and zinc ions. It may also possess bactericidal or antitumor properties. A specific folding variant of human alpha-lactalbumin, known as HAMLET, can form in acidic environments such as the stomach. HAMLET is believed to induce apoptosis in tumor cells and immature cells. The folding dynamics of alpha-lactalbumin are therefore highly unusual. When alpha-lactalbumin forms a complex with Gal-T1, a galactosyltransferase, it significantly enhances the enzyme's affinity for glucose—by approximately 1000-fold—while inhibiting its ability to polymerize multiple galactose units. This interaction facilitates the conversion of Gal-T1 into lactose synthase, thereby creating a pathway for lactose formation. Physical Properties The structure of alpha-lactalbumin is well-characterized and consists of 123 amino acids and four disulfide bridges. One of the key structural differences between alpha-lactalbumin and beta-lactoglobulin is the absence of any free thiol groups in alpha-lactalbumin. This absence prevents it from serving as a starting point for covalent aggregation reactions. Consequently, pure alpha-lactalbumin does not form gels upon denaturation and acidification. Evolution The amino acid sequence of alpha-lactalbumin shows a strong similarity to that of lysozymes, particularly the calcium-binding c-lysozyme. This suggests that alpha-lactalbumin likely evolved through gene duplication of the c-lysozyme gene, followed by subsequent mutations. The gene encoding alpha-lactalbumin predates the last common ancestor of mammals and birds, placing its evolutionary origin at approximately 300 million years ago.
